To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified novel immunogenic regions of human herpesvirus-8 lytic and latent proteins and demonstrated that these regions can activate polyfunctional CD8 T cells in healthy HHV8 seropositive individuals, suggesting that these T cells may be important in control of HHV8 infection.

we have identified 12 novel CD8(+) cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) epitopes in the lytic and latency genes of human herpesvirus-8 and that these epitopes activate monofunctional as well as polyfunctional CTLs in healthy individuals.
we identified novel immunogenic regions of HHV- 8 lytic proteins (gB and K8. 1) and latency proteins (LANA-1 and K12) that could be important in CD8(+)T cell control of HH V-8 infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying immunogenic regions of the HHV-8 genome that could be important in controlling HHV8 infection and preventing the development of HHV- 8-associated malignancies.
understanding the immunogenicity and the functional properties of CD8(+) HHV-8 specific T cells in healthy HHV8-seroposive individuals.
identifying the epitopes of HHV- 8 proteins that activate CD8(+)T cells to produce a variety of effector molecules that may play a role in controlling the virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CD8( ) T cells are important for the control of HHV 8.
the CD8+ T lymphocytes are the main effectors of immune control of HHV8 infection.
the HHV-8 proteins gB, K8.1 (orf K8.1), LANA-1 and K12 (orf K12) are all immunogenic in HHV-8 infected healthy subjects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HHV-8 has many potential targets for CD8+ T cells to recognize, and these targets could potentially play an important role for the development of vaccines and immunotherapies.
the immune system is able to detect and respond to multiple regions of the HHV-8 genome.
we have identified a number of new immunodominant HHV-8 peptides and that these peptides elicit a variety of CD8(+) polyfunctional T cell responses in healthy individuals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified novel immunogenic regions in the HHV-8 viral genome that can be used as vaccine candidates.
HHV-8 has a number of immunogenic regions that could potentially be used to design a vaccine to prevent HHV-8-associated malignancies.
HHV-8 elicits CD8+ T cells that produce multiple cytokines and that HHV- 8 infection is controlled by the immune system.
